1:
The opening verses are read mainly against their parallel. Ellicott notes that the first coincides with the account in Kings but drops the note dating the accession to the seventh year of Jehu, and that Joash is a contraction of Jehoash, a name meaning either that Iahu is fire or, more probably, that Iahu is a man. Where Kings has all his days, while Jehoiada instructed him, he observes that all his days is of course relative to the clause following it and that the chronicler has given the meaning accurately. The two wives he finds absent from the parallel altogether, doubtless drawn by the compiler from another source, Kings carrying in that place the note that the high places were not taken away. Clarke works the arithmetic instead: having been hidden six years in the temple and being seven at his accession, the boy can have been only a year old when his aunt secreted him. Delitzsch refers the repair that follows to his own commentary on Kings, where the formal divergences and the essential agreement of the two narratives are set out.

Who took the wives, and why, is the one point of substance. Gill insists they were not for Jehoiada, who already had a wife, the king's own aunt, besides sons who had joined him in the anointing, and who was by now upwards of a hundred years old; he advised the marriages and proposed the women himself once the king came of age, having watched the mischief done in church and state alike when Jehoram married Athaliah. One of them, Gill adds, was Jehoadan, and the other's name is not known. Henry takes the same facts as a lesson for the young, that it is a happiness to be set out in life under the direction of the wise and good, and especially prudent to take advice in marriage as Joash did in leaving the choice to his guardian, since Jezebel and Athaliah had been such plagues; he that will not be counselled, Henry says, cannot be helped. But Henry also reads the arrangement as a warning: men may go far in the external performances of religion, and keep long to them, merely by the power of their education and the influence of their friends, while having no hearty affection for divine things nor any inward relish of them.
4:
The order to collect, and the slackness that met it, open the account. Ellicott prefers restore to repair as the modern equivalent, thinks the chronicler has paraphrased an account that is not very clear, and notes the Levites are not mentioned in Kings at all; the order to go out to the cities is his reading of the instruction there that the priests take it each from his own acquaintance, and that the Levites hastened not agrees with the note that by the twenty-third year the breaches were unrepaired, the remissness of the priestly order being inferable. Clarke explains the dilapidation, the house pillaged under Joram and Athaliah to enrich the temple of Baal and then left to decay, and calls this the first general collection for repairing a house of God. The title given to Jehoiada then divides them. Wesley observes he is not called chief priest or high priest but only the chief, which he might be by nearness to the royal family or as head of one of the twenty-four families; Gill allows all of these and makes him in effect prime minister of state; Ellicott reads simply the head of the sacerdotal caste.

Two phrases in the sixth and seventh verses produce flat contradictions. Clarke identifies the collection of Moses with the half-shekel poll-tax on every man from twenty years old upward, reckoned a ransom for their souls that no plague should come among them. Ellicott denies it: the tax of Moses is not that poll-tax but a general designation of the moneys named in the parallel. On the sons of Athaliah, Ellicott takes them for Ahaziah and his elder brothers, gratifying the queen's hatred of the exclusive worship of Jehovah, and guesses that parts of the buildings were pulled down to make room for a temple of Baal; Wesley agrees and reads the breaking up of both the treasuries and the house itself; Gill flatly refuses the identification, following Kimchi in making them sons of Athaliah by another man.

The chest and the proclamation follow in language peculiar to this book. Ellicott notes that Kings has Jehoiada take a chest and bore a hole in its lid, details characteristic of a more original account, and places this one in the court just inside the gate; making a proclamation is literally uttering a voice in Judah, a phrase found here only in that sense; and the two verses which follow are the chronicler's own, their author being fond of dwelling on how willingly the people gave in the good old time, doubtless by way of suggestion to his contemporaries. Ellicott observes that the Levites are again given their part, and that the high priest's officer stands here where Kings has the high priest himself, seemingly in the interest of a dignity that had grown as the monarchy receded.

The work and the surplus close it. Ellicott makes those in charge Levitical inspectors of works who hired masons and carpenters from time to time, and dwells on the metaphor of the thirteenth verse, where the work perfected is literally a bandage applied to it, an expression used again of the walls of Jerusalem and before that by Jeremiah of national restoration; setting the house in his state is rather making it stand according to its measure. Over the surplus the two part company, Delitzsch having the king cause the vessels to be made and Ellicott giving that to Jehoiada. Ellicott then meets the difficulty that Kings denies any such vessels were made, supposing the earlier writer reports what was done with the money while repairs were in progress and the chronicler accounts for what was left at the end, while admitting the appearance of contradiction is curious enough to suggest the didactic aims of the later historian. Wesley settles it in a line: new vessels, because Athaliah and her sons had carried off the old.
15:
Jehoiada dies full of years, and his age detains Ellicott. He renders it literally, that Jehoiada became old and was satisfied with days, a verb so used only here and once before, where the older expression was adjectival; and on the hundred and thirty he canvasses physiology, reporting a modern limit of a hundred and five with one academician allowing half a century beyond it, and concludes the age is not impossible, though an error of transcription is not impossible either. Clarke says he had in fact been king, governing in Joash's name, so a royal burial measures the estimation he was held in; Ellicott adds the stated reason, that he had done good, and perhaps the regency and the royal marriage. Henry takes the encomium for a gravestone inscription and calls it the greatest honour to do good in one's generation; Wesley supplies the sting, that the little religion Joash had was all buried in that grave.

The apostasy follows, and Henry diagnoses rather than narrates it: the king had never been sincere, never acted from principle but in compliance with the man who had helped him to the crown, so that when the wind turned he turned with it. Ellicott reads the obeisance as asking a boon whose nature the next verse makes plain, the royal sanction of forms of worship they hankered after; Delitzsch says the same, that the request is nowhere stated but may be gathered from what they did, and that the king did not venture to deny them. Wesley supplies the pretext, that they asked not to be confined to journeys to Jerusalem but to have their fathers' liberty of the high places, and could then worship idols undisturbed. Ellicott objects to the rendering groves and notes that a sin of the nobles, allowed and perhaps imitated by the king, drew the nation into its penal consequences; both he and Delitzsch identify the wrath with the Syrian invasion still to be narrated.

Prophets are sent and ignored, which Gill reads as clemency exercised before wrath. Henry says it is the work of ministers to bring people not to themselves but to God, and that in the most degenerate times God left not himself without witness, so that those who perish are inexcusable: few would hear the prophets, fewer heed them, fewest believe them. On Zechariah he observes that the Spirit clothed or invested him, that the priest is an epithet of Jehoiada and not of the son, that he probably stood on the steps of the inner court facing the people in the outer, and that the last clause runs rather for ye have forsaken the Lord, and he hath forsaken you. Clarke gives the Targum's fuller scene, the king and people burning incense to an idol on the day of expiation and keeping the priests from their offerings; Wesley places the prophet in one of the desks of the priests' court.

The stoning draws the sharpest comment. Ellicott notes that stoning was the legal penalty for idolatry, and guesses the words had been represented to the king as treasonable, the Syrian threat perhaps already in the air, so that it would be easy to allege the prophet's wish was father to his thought. He and Delitzsch agree that this is the Zacharias whose murder Christ names, Matthew 23:35, Delitzsch calling it the last prophet-murder the Old Testament narrates and both noting the father named there is not Jehoiada, Ellicott suggesting Barachias was the father. Wesley reports the Jewish reckoning of seven transgressions in one: a priest, a prophet and a judge killed, innocent blood shed, and the court, the Sabbath and the day of expiation polluted. Ellicott finds the dying imprecation in keeping with a dispensation that exacted blood for blood, and sets it against the prayer of Stephen; Clarke and Delitzsch note how soon it was answered.
23:
The invasion arrives within the year, and the speed of it is the first thing noted. Gill observes that the prophecy had its accomplishment so soon; Wesley presses harder, that God so quickly heard the cry of his prophet's blood and revenged it, the princes being singled out so it might appear they were directed by God against the first beginners of the apostasy. Ellicott works the military detail: the phrase is at the running out of the year, and only a small part of a besieging army seems to have been detached against Jerusalem, the princes of Judah meeting it in the field with a large force and being routed, the Syrians apparently aiming to cut off the leaders. The spoil went to Hazael, probably still at Gath with his main body, so that the apostate princes were overtaken by the prophetic doom.

The twenty-fourth verse Ellicott treats as explaining the twenty-third, rendering it that with fewness of men the host of Syria had come and Jehovah had given into their hand a host in exceeding abundance, the phrase occurring nowhere else. Gill says the same in a clause: it consisted but of few. He notes that the parallel has Hazael intending to march on Jerusalem himself until Joash bribed his forbearance with the treasures of temple and palace, and that executing judgment is always used of divine requital. He concludes that this narrative views the invasion from a religious standpoint, omitting details the earlier book specifies while keeping whatever points its moral, such as the destruction of the idolatrous princes and the rout of a great host by a small company.

On the king's end the readings part. Ellicott refuses to take the great diseases for battle wounds, since the text never says Joash was wounded, only that the loss of his princes was a judgment on him; the word occurs here alone and probably means pains, so either calamity brought on the sickness or the invasion found him already prostrate. On the blood of the sons of Jehoiada he notes that the Greek and Vulgate correct the plural to a singular, meaning Zechariah, and that it is more probably rhetorical than a slip: the writer does not mean that revenge for Jehoiada's posterity moved the conspirators, but that their deed was a judgment on the king for that crime. Wesley reads the plural at face value, inferring that Joash had killed Zechariah's brothers as well and that the murderers perhaps meant to avenge that innocent blood, whatever God intended in permitting it. Both note that the burial withheld the royal sepulchres.

The assassins and the source close the chapter. Clarke observes that neither man was a Jew, one mother an Ammonitess and the other a Moabitess, supposes they were foreigners of the king's chamber with easy access, and turns it into a complaint that kings have long made confidants of foreigners to their cost. Ellicott prefers the forms in Kings and then disposes of two commentators: one is wrong to claim the chronicler substituted the mothers' names for the fathers', and another even knows why the epithets were added, namely to show an idolatrous lapse avenged by two sons of idolatrous wives, which Ellicott calls fancy determined by prejudice. The additions rather indicate the use of a source other than the canonical book of Kings, as does the strikingly original account of Zechariah's death, and the next verse names that source. On the burdens, Clarke suggests the Syrian tribute, though some think the sums amassed for the temple; Wesley makes them the judgments by Syrians and sickness alike; Ellicott offers a threatening prophecy used collectively, or a tribute, and rejects the Hebrew margin. Clarke closes on the lost original, this midrash being gone like Trogus Pompeius in forty-four volumes, surviving only in the abridgment that destroyed it.
